clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in RASA1 (CM-AVM1) or EPHB4 (CM-AVM2)
The cutaneous hallmark is multiple small, round-to-oval, pink-red capillary malformations, often with a pale halo, scattered over the body
A minority of patients harbour fast-flow lesions, namely arteriovenous malformations or fistulae, which may involve the skin, muscle, bone or central nervous system
High-flow shunting through an AVM can cause pain, bleeding, tissue overgrowth or, when intracranial or spinal, serious neurological events
The multifocal small capillary stains differ from the single large segmental port-wine stain of Sturge-Weber syndrome
Parkes-Weber syndrome (a limb with capillary staining, overgrowth and high-flow AV shunting) lies within the RASA1-related spectrum
EPHB4-related disease may overlap phenotypically with hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
Family screening and consideration of central nervous system imaging are important because AVMs may be clinically silent
reference.pathophysiology: Capillary malformation-AVM syndrome results from germline loss-of-function variants in RASA1 or EPHB4, genes that regulate RAS-MAPK signalling in vascular endothelium and thereby control the balance between arterial, venous and capillary differentiation. A second somatic hit in affected vessels is thought to precipitate individual lesions, explaining the multifocal and variable phenotype. Most lesions are the small multifocal capillary malformations, but the same signalling disturbance can produce fast-flow arteriovenous malformations and fistulae capable of significant shunting and their attendant complications.
additionalDifferentials: Parkes-Weber syndrome (considered part of the RASA1 spectrum)
Multiple isolated capillary malformations without a syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing for RASA1 and EPHB4 variants
Doppler ultrasound to identify fast-flow within cutaneous lesions
MRI/MRA to characterise and localise arteriovenous malformations
Brain and spine imaging to screen for central nervous system AVMs
Echocardiography if high-output cardiac effects are suspected
Family history review and cascade screening of relatives
redFlags: Neurological symptoms suggesting an intracranial or spinal arteriovenous malformation
High-output cardiac failure from large AV shunting
Bleeding or ulceration of a fast-flow lesion
Rapid limb enlargement or overgrowth (Parkes-Weber pattern)
New bruit or thrill over a previously stable lesion
reference.prognosis: Most affected individuals have only benign multifocal capillary stains and a good prognosis, but the presence of a fast-flow arteriovenous malformation, particularly in the brain or spine, can lead to serious or life-threatening complications; lifelong awareness and targeted surveillance are advised for gene carriers.
pitfalls: Dismissing multiple small capillary stains as trivial and missing the underlying diagnosis
Failing to screen for occult central nervous system arteriovenous malformations
Confusing the multifocal lesions with a single Sturge-Weber port-wine stain
Not offering genetic counselling and family screening for an autosomal dominant condition
references: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Haemangiomas and Malformations
management: Molecular genetic testing for RASA1 and EPHB4 variants to establish the diagnosis
Brain and spine imaging to screen for central nervous system arteriovenous malformations because of the haemorrhage risk
Doppler ultrasound to detect fast-flow within cutaneous lesions, with MRI/MRA to localise arteriovenous malformations
Embolisation or surgical resection of symptomatic high-flow lesions through a vascular anomalies team
Pulsed dye laser for cosmetically significant capillary stains
Echocardiography and cardiac review if high-output effects from large shunts are suspected
Genetic counselling and cascade screening of at-risk relatives given autosomal dominant inheritance
